questions.question: What timestamp anchors feature availability for a training example?
options: The completion timestamp of the dataset build job that assembled the example
The wall-clock time at which the training job first reads the feature table
The maturity timestamp at which the example's label finally became known
The prediction cutoff timestamp at which the example would have been scored

questions.question: What does a point-in-time join select?
options: The latest feature record for the entity available by the example's cutoff
The newest feature record for the entity as of the day the dataset was built
Every feature version recorded for the entity, leaving one row for each version
The first feature record for the entity that was written after its label matured

questions.question: Feature C42 has values 3 at 09:00 and 5 at 11:00. What value joins to a 10:00 prediction?
options: Both
Null

questions.question: Why store both event time and availability time?
options: Because event time replaces the entity key when features are joined by interval
Because a fact can describe an earlier moment yet become usable only later
Because availability time is what determines whether a label window has matured
Because the two timestamps are always identical, so either one can be used

questions.question: A lab sample is collected at 09:00 but published at 14:00. Can an 11:00 production prediction use it?
options: Yes, because its event time of 09:00 falls before the prediction timestamp
No, because a prediction may only use facts published on an earlier calendar day
Yes, because training runs long after both the collection and the publication
No, because the value had not yet been published to the serving system at 11:00

questions.question: Why can an end-of-day feature snapshot be wrong for a noon prediction?
options: Because it excludes every change made before noon, leaving the feature undefined
Because it can fold in changes made after noon that serving could not see
Because it rounds each entity's timestamp to midnight, which breaks the join
Because it retains only the newest schema, so older feature columns are dropped

questions.topic: Label Leakage: Learning from the Future
questions.question: What is label leakage?
options: A feature with many null values, so the model ends up learning from missingness
A model whose training accuracy sits far below its accuracy on the test set
A training input carrying information unavailable at scoring time or encoding the label
A label that is missing in production, so the serving path has to impute it from features

questions.topic: Label Leakage: Learning from the Future
questions.question: Which support-ticket feature is likely to leak escalation?
options: The resolution team recorded on the ticket, which is assigned after an escalation
The product category the customer chose on the ticket creation form
The free-text description the customer typed when first opening the ticket
The hour of the day on which the ticket was first submitted to the queue

questions.topic: Label Leakage: Learning from the Future
questions.question: Why fit imputation and normalization only on the training fold?
options: Because the training fold is the only fold guaranteed to contain no missing values at all
Because normalization constants are what determine the label of each example
Because validation and test folds are scored without applying any transformation
Because fitting on the whole dataset lets validation and test distributions leak in

questions.topic: Label Leakage: Learning from the Future
questions.question: Why is random row splitting risky for repeated customers?
options: Because a random split always produces test folds far too small to measure anything
Because one customer's near-identical examples can land on both sides of the split
Because temporal splits are the only splits that carry labels for the later periods
Because a customer contributing many rows will dominate the overall training loss

questions.topic: Label Leakage: Learning from the Future
questions.question: How should target encoding be computed for training rows?
options: From the category average taken over the full dataset, including the test labels
From the maximum label observed in each category, which bounds the encoded value
From out-of-fold statistics that exclude the row's own target from the average
From the row's own target, blended with the global mean to smooth rare categories

questions.topic: Label Leakage: Learning from the Future
questions.question: Why can examples near the dataset end need exclusion?
options: Because their identifiers are the largest, so hash-based splitting assigns them badly
Because features computed for them have not yet been written to the offline store
Because temporal data cannot be split once the observation window has closed
Because their label window has not fully elapsed, so the outcome is not settled yet

questions.question: What is training-serving skew?
options: A feature that takes different values or meanings offline and online for one prediction
A model that has been given far more training rows than held-out evaluation rows
An online store whose point reads return in milliseconds while training scans run for hours
A feature definition pinned to one shared version across training and serving

questions.question: What should a feature definition specify besides its name?
options: Its dashboard color, chart type, refresh icon, and the team that owns that panel
Its online read latency, cache hit rate, replica count, and storage engine choice
Its sources, transformation, keys, timestamp logic, null policy, type, and version
Its contribution to the model score, permutation importance, and rank among features

questions.question: What does a parity test do?
options: It counts production requests per feature and alerts when the rate moves sharply
It runs the offline and online paths on identical inputs and compares their outputs
It compares two model versions on one holdout set and reports the score difference
It deletes feature rows whose freshness has passed the declared maximum age

questions.question: Why bind a model artifact to feature versions?
options: Because two feature versions cannot be materialized side by side during a rollout
Because the newest feature version is always compatible with any deployed model
Because a model artifact stores no features itself and must fetch them at load time
Because a model trained against version 3 can misread values produced by version 4

questions.question: Offline missing values are null, while online missing values become zero. What is the likely consequence?
options: A semantic skew, because the model reads the zero as a real value rather than as absent
Exact parity, because most models treat a null and a zero as the same input value
Faster training, because null handling is skipped once the values become numeric
An automatic missing indicator, because the store flags each substituted default value

questions.question: What should training do when online features necessarily arrive with delay and missingness?
options: Train on the corrected values that arrived later, since they are the accurate truth
Strip the feature timestamps so the training job cannot depend on arrival order
Reproduce the same delay and missingness in the features it trains on
Train on the freshest historical values and assume that serving latency will improve
